In terms of electricity requirement for liquefaction processes, hydrogen liquefaction can require up to 0.45 kWh electricity per kilowatt-hour of LH on a lower heating value basis, while LNG 2 and LE are more on the order of 0.01 kWh to 0.04 kWh electricity per kilowatt-hour of fuel. If a small-scale hydrogen liquefaction facility of 10 MTPD of LH (capable of fueling 10 or more 2 regional LH turboprop aircraft daily) with 15 kWh/kg LH electricity input were constructed at 2 2 an airport, it would require a power input of 6.25 MW. Similarly sized LNG and LE production facilities on an energy output basis would require only about 2%–4% of this power input. In comparison, a typical large hub airport has a grid interconnection capacity around 10 MW to 40 MW (Semchukova et al. 2025; Airport Cooperative Research Program n.d.; Zellers and Bradford 2025). It is also worth mentioning that electrolytic hydrogen production requires about 55 kWh/kg of gaseous H produced, requiring an average power of 23 MW at 10 MTPD H . If an 2 2 airport did pursue building its own electrolytic hydrogen production and liquefaction infrastructure, it would almost certainly need to expand its grid interconnection capacity. Possible methods to deliver and dispense these cryogenic fuels into aircraft are largely the same in a general sense. Again, where differences appear are in material selections and infrastructure design and operations. LH systems will again be more complex than LNG and LE systems 2 because of the more extreme temperature state and small size of the LH molecule. Differences 2 in thermal, physical, and chemical properties of each of these fuels may also lead to differences in standard operating procedures once aircraft operating on these cryogenic fuels reach the market. As an example, it is still not clear if any of these cryogenic fuels could be dispensed into an aircraft while the aircraft is at a terminal gate with passengers boarding or disembarking, or if a designated refueling location away from the terminal is necessary. In addition, personnel will need special training for managing cryogenic liquids to ensure safe tarmac operation. Through the full supply chain from production to dispensing and storage on board an aircraft, the leakage pathways and mitigation strategies are also similar for LH , LNG, and LE. Figure 42 2 illustrates the most common leakage pathway for hydrogen supply chains, which for the most part apply to LNG and LE. Permeation and diffusion are the two leakage mechanisms that apply least to LNG and LE because of the larger size of these molecules.
